'''John Torrence Tate Jr.''' (March 13, 1925&nbsp;– October 16, 2019) was an American mathematician distinguished for many fundamental contributions in [[algebraic number theory]], [[arithmetic geometry]], and related areas in [[algebraic geometry]]. He was awarded the [[Abel Prize]] in 2010.

== Biography ==
Tate was born in [[Minneapolis]], on March 13, 1925. His father, [[John Torrence Tate Sr.|John Tate Sr.]], was a professor of physics at the [[University of Minnesota]] and a longtime editor of ''[[Physical Review]]''. His mother, Lois Beatrice Fossler, was a high school English teacher. Tate Jr. received his bachelor's degree in mathematics in 1946 from [[Harvard University]] and entered the doctoral program in physics at [[Princeton University]]. He later transferred to the [[Princeton University Department of Mathematics|mathematics department]] and received his PhD in mathematics in 1950 after completing a doctoral dissertation titled [[Tate's thesis|"Fourier analysis in number fields and Hecke's zeta functions"]] under the supervision of [[Emil Artin]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Tate|first=John Torrence|url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/1776346|title=Fourier analysis in number fields and Hecke's zeta functions|date=1950|language=en}}</ref> Tate taught at Harvard for 36 years before joining the [[University of Texas]] in 1990 as a Sid W. Richardson Foundation Regents Chair.<ref>{{MacTutor|id=Tate}}</ref> He retired from the Texas mathematics department in 2009 and returned to Harvard as a professor emeritus.<ref name="stat"/>

Tate died at his home in [[Lexington, Massachusetts]] on October 16, 2019, aged 94.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/28/science/john-t-tate-dead.html|title=John T. Tate, Familiar Name in the World of Numbers, Dies at 94|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=October 28, 2019}}</ref><ref name=harvard>{{Cite web|url=http://www.math.harvard.edu/history/tate/index.html |publisher=Harvard |title=John Tate, 1925–2019 |date=October 17, 2019 |access-date=October 17, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://news.utexas.edu/2019/10/18/remembering-eminent-ut-austin-mathematician-john-tate/ |title=Remembering Eminent UT Austin Mathematician John Tate |date=October 18, 2019 |access-date=October 19, 2019}}</ref>

== Mathematical work ==
[[Tate's thesis]] (1950) on [[Fourier analysis]] in [[Algebraic number field|number fields]] has become one of the ingredients for the modern theory of [[automorphic form]]s and their [[L-function]]s, notably by its use of the [[adele ring]], its self-duality and harmonic analysis on it; independently and a little earlier, [[Kenkichi Iwasawa]] obtained a similar theory. Together with his advisor [[Emil Artin]], Tate gave a cohomological treatment of [[Class field theory|global class field theory]] using techniques of [[group cohomology]] applied to the [[Adelic algebraic group|idele class group]] and [[Galois cohomology]].<ref name="xin">{{Cite web|url=http://news.xinhuanet.com/english2010/sci/2010-03/25/c_13223596.htm|title=American mathematician John Tate wins 2010 Abel Prize|publisher=Xinhua.net|date=2010-03-25|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100822035034/http://news.xinhuanet.com/english2010/sci/2010-03/25/c_13223596.htm|archive-date=2010-08-22}}</ref> This treatment made more transparent some of the algebraic structures in the previous approaches to class field theory, which used central division algebras to compute the [[Brauer group]] of a [[global field]].

Subsequently, Tate introduced what are now known as [[Tate cohomology group]]s. In the decades following that discovery he extended the reach of Galois cohomology with the [[Tate duality|Poitou–Tate duality]], the [[Tate–Shafarevich group]], and relations with [[algebraic K-theory]]. With [[Jonathan Lubin]], he recast [[local class field theory]] by the use of [[Formal group law|formal groups]], creating the [[Lubin–Tate formal group law|Lubin–Tate local theory]] of [[complex multiplication]].

He has also made a number of individual and important contributions to [[p-adic number|''p''-adic]] theory; for example, Tate's invention of [[rigid analytic space]]s can be said to have spawned the entire field of [[rigid analytic space|rigid analytic geometry]]. He found a ''p''-adic analogue of [[Hodge theory]], now called [[Hodge–Tate module|Hodge–Tate theory]], which has blossomed into another central technique of modern [[algebraic number theory]].<ref name="xin" /> Other innovations of his include the "[[Tate curve]]" parametrization for certain ''p''-adic [[elliptic curve]]s and the [[Barsotti–Tate group|''p''-divisible (Tate–Barsotti) groups]].

Many of his results were not immediately published and some of them were written up by [[Serge Lang]], [[Jean-Pierre Serre]], [[Joseph H. Silverman]] and others. Tate and Serre collaborated on a paper on [[Glossary of arithmetic and diophantine geometry#G|good reduction]] of [[abelian variety|abelian varieties]]. The classification of abelian varieties over [[finite field]]s was carried out by [[Taira Honda]] and Tate (the [[Honda–Tate theorem]]).<ref>J.T. Tate, "Classes d'isogénie des variétés abéliennes sur un corps fini (d' après T. Honda)", Sem. Bourbaki Exp. 352, Lect. notes in math., 179, Springer (1971)</ref>

The [[Tate conjecture]]s are the equivalent for [[étale cohomology]] of the [[Hodge conjecture]]. They relate to the Galois action on the ℓ-adic cohomology of an algebraic variety, identifying a space of "[[Tate cycle]]s" (the fixed cycles for a suitably [[Tate twist|Tate-twisted]] action) that conjecturally picks out the algebraic cycles. A special case of the conjectures, which are open in the general case, was involved in the proof of the [[Faltings' theorem|Mordell conjecture]] by [[Gerd Faltings]].

Tate has also had a major influence on the development of number theory through his role as a Ph.D. advisor. His students include [[George Bergman]], [[Ted Chinburg]], [[Bernard Dwork]], [[Benedict Gross]], [[Robert Kottwitz]], [[Jonathan Lubin]], [[Stephen Lichtenbaum]], [[James Milne (mathematician)|James Milne]], [[V. Kumar Murty]], [[Carl Pomerance]], [[Ken Ribet]], [[Joseph H. Silverman]], [[Dinesh Thakur (mathematician)|Dinesh Thakur]], and [[William C. Waterhouse]].

== Awards and honors ==
In 1956, Tate was awarded the [[American Mathematical Society]]'s [[Cole Prize]] for outstanding contributions to number theory. He was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1958.<ref>{{Cite web |title=John Torrence Tate, Jr. |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/john-torrence-tate-jr |access-date=2023-04-28 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |language=en}}</ref> He was elected to the United States [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1969.<ref>{{Cite web |title=John T. Tate |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/john-t-tate-5rjhfy/ |access-date=2023-04-28 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref> In 1992, he was elected as Foreign Member of the French Académie des Sciences. In 1995, he received the [[Leroy P. Steele Prize|Leroy P. Steele Prize for Lifetime Achievement]] from the American Mathematical Society. He was awarded a [[Wolf Prize in Mathematics]] in 2002/03 for his creation of fundamental concepts in [[algebraic number theory]].<ref>[http://www.wolffund.org.il/full.asp?id=83 The 2002/3 Wolf Foundation Prize in Mathematics.] [[Wolf Foundation]]. Accessed March 24, 2010.</ref> In 2012, he became a fellow of the American Mathematical Society.<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2013-08-25.</ref>

{{Quote box|align=right|width=33%|quote = I got a phone call at 7 in the morning from a guy with a very strong Norwegian accent. That was the first I heard of it. I feel very fortunate. I realize that there is any number of people they could have chosen.|source=—&nbsp;John Tate<ref name="stat" />}}

In 2010, the [[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]], of which he was a member,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.dnva.no/c26849/artikkel/vis.html?tid=40116 |title=Gruppe 1: Matematiske fag |publisher=[[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]] |language=no |access-date=7 October 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131110152102/http://www.dnva.no/c26849/artikkel/vis.html?tid=40116 |archive-date=10 November 2013}}</ref> awarded him the [[Abel Prize]], citing "his vast and lasting impact on the theory of numbers". According to a release by the Abel Prize committee, "Many of the major lines of research in [[algebraic number theory]] and [[arithmetic geometry]] are only possible because of the incisive contributions and illuminating insights of John Tate. He has truly left a conspicuous imprint on modern mathematics."<ref name="ab">{{Cite web |editor= |title=2010: John Torrence Tate |url=https://abelprize.no/abel-prize-laureates/2010 |publisher=The Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters}}</ref>

Tate has been described as "one of the seminal mathematicians for the past half-century" by [[William Beckner (mathematician)|William Beckner]], Chairman of the Department of Mathematics at the [[University of Texas at Austin]].<ref name="stat">{{Cite web|url=http://www.statesman.com/news/local/retired-ut-mathematician-wins-prestigious-abel-prize-441915.html|title=Retired UT mathematician wins prestigious Abel Prize|author=Ralph K.M. Haurwitz|date=March 24, 2010|publisher=Statesman.com|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100326222752/http://www.statesman.com/news/local/retired-ut-mathematician-wins-prestigious-abel-prize-441915.html|archive-date=March 26, 2010}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Tate married twice. His first wife was Karin Artin, his doctoral advisor's daughter. Together they had three daughters, six grandchildren, and a great-grandson. One of his grandchildren, [[Dustin Clausen]], is a professor of mathematics at the [[Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques]]. After Tate divorced, he married Carol MacPherson.<ref name="harvard2">{{Cite web|url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2020/10/john-tate-94/|title=John Tate, 94|date=7 October 2020 |publisher=The Harvard Gazette}}</ref>
